transcript.content: Hello, thank you for coming in. Can you tell me what’s been bothering you or what brings you here today?

Yeah, um… I guess what brings me in is that people keep acting like I’m overthinking something, but I don’t think I am. It’s about my father’s death and the stuff around it afterward. I’ve gone through the hospital records, the emails about donations, the timing of things, and everyone keeps telling me it all lines up, that it’s just paperwork and automated messages and normal delays, but when I actually compare the timestamps and what’s missing, it doesn’t look normal to me.

There are attachments that should be there and aren’t, or emails that refer to things I never received. And then when I ask certain people in the community about it, they get vague or they avoid answering directly. It’s not like I’m saying I have every piece of the puzzle, but that’s kind of the point — pieces are missing. And everyone wants me to just accept the official version, but it feels obvious to me that someone is hiding what really happened. I know that probably sounds like I’m fixating on details, but the details are where the truth is.
Do you believe that someone intentionally altered or concealed information about your father's death, despite others telling you there's no evidence of that?

Yes. I mean… yes, I do. I know people keep saying there’s no evidence, but to me that depends on what they’re willing to count as evidence. When I line up the hospital records with the donation emails and the timestamps, there are gaps that don’t make sense. There are messages that refer to attachments I never got, or things that should have been included but just aren’t there. And then everyone acts like that’s normal, like I’m supposed to shrug it off.

It’s not just one typo or one delayed email. It’s the pattern. The timing, the missing pieces, the way certain people in the community get vague when I ask direct questions. They’ll answer around it, or say they don’t remember, or tell me I should let it go. That doesn’t feel like nothing to me.

So, yes, I believe someone concealed something, or altered what was available afterward. I’m not saying I know every single person involved or exactly how they did it, but I can’t accept that all of those inconsistencies are accidental. It feels obvious to me that someone is hiding what really happened around my father’s death.
Do you believe that the people who are hiding this information are part of a larger group or organization working together to keep the truth from you?

I don’t know if I’d call it a formal organization, exactly. I’m not saying there’s some big named group with meetings and minutes or anything like that. But do I think more than one person knows, or that people are sort of protecting each other? Yes, that’s what it looks like to me.

Because if it were just one mistake in the hospital records, or one weird donation email, I could maybe accept that. But it’s the way the timestamps don’t quite match, and then the attachments that are referenced but not actually there, and then when I ask people in the community direct questions, they suddenly get vague. They don’t answer the thing I actually asked. They tell me it all lines up, or that I’m reading too much into it, but they don’t explain the missing pieces.

So… larger group? I don’t know how large. I can’t prove some structured organization. But it feels coordinated enough that I don’t think it’s accidental. Someone is hiding what really happened around my father’s death, and other people seem to be helping keep it quiet, even if they’re not all officially “part” of something.
Have you ever seen, heard, or sensed something that others around you didn’t seem to notice?

I don’t think so. I mean, not in the sense of seeing things that other people can’t see, or hearing voices or something like that. That’s not really what this is.

Sometimes I notice things other people don’t seem to notice, but I mean details — like an email time being off, or a record not matching, or someone’s wording changing when I ask them something. Other people may not pick up on that, or they dismiss it, but it’s not like I’m sensing some presence in the room or hearing something no one else hears.

So… no, I wouldn’t say I’ve had that. It’s more that I’m paying attention to things other people either miss or don’t want to look at.
Have you ever had thoughts or beliefs that others have told you aren’t true, but you still feel certain about them even without clear proof?

Yes… I guess that’s exactly what people tell me. They say I don’t have “clear proof,” or they say the hospital records and the donation emails all line up, but I don’t see how they can say that if they’re actually looking at the same things I’m looking at.

When I compare the timestamps, there are things that don’t match the way they should. And there are emails that refer to attachments that aren’t there, or records that seem like they should include something but don’t. Then when I ask certain people in the community about it, they don’t just say, “Here’s the explanation.” They avoid the question, or answer something adjacent to it, or act like I’m being unreasonable for noticing it in the first place.

So yes, people tell me it isn’t true, or that I’m reading too much into it. But to me it’s obvious someone is hiding what really happened around my father’s death. I know I can’t hand you one single document that proves the whole thing from start to finish, but the pattern is there. I feel certain about that.
Have you ever had a strong belief about something happening in your life — like a plot or cover-up — that turned out to be completely false, but you were absolutely sure of it at the time?

Completely false? No… I don’t think I’d say that. I understand why people want to put it in that category, like, “You were sure, and then later you found out you were wrong,” but that hasn’t happened here.

What’s happened is people keep telling me the hospital records and the donation emails all line up, and that there’s nothing there. But when I sit down and actually compare them — the timestamps, the missing attachments, the references to things that aren’t included — it doesn’t look clean to me. It looks like pieces have been left out or shifted around. And then when I ask certain people in the community direct questions, they don’t answer directly. They kind of sidestep it, or they act like I’m making trouble just by asking.

So I can’t point to a time where I was absolutely sure about something like this and then it turned out to be completely false. With my father’s death, I still think someone is hiding what really happened. I know everyone says I don’t have the one piece of proof that would settle it, but to me the pattern is obvious.
Even though others have shown you records or explanations that contradict your belief, do you still feel certain that someone is hiding the truth about your father's death, without any doubt?

Yes. I mean… I know how that sounds when you say “without any doubt,” but yes, I still feel certain.

People keep saying the records explain it, or that the hospital paperwork and the donation emails all match up, but when I actually compare them, they don’t feel consistent to me. The timestamps don’t line up the way they should. There are references to attachments that aren’t there, or things that seem like they should be documented but are just missing. And it isn’t just the documents — it’s the way certain people answer when I ask about it. They don’t give a straightforward explanation. They avoid the specific question, or they make me feel like I’m being inappropriate for even noticing.

So no, I don’t really see those explanations as contradicting it. To me, they feel like part of the problem — like they’re trying to make it look settled when it isn’t. I know everyone wants me to accept that there’s nothing hidden, but when I look at the pattern, it’s obvious to me that someone is hiding what really happened around my father’s death.
Can you think of any kind of evidence or explanation that would convince you that no one was hiding the truth about your father's death?

I’ve thought about that a lot, actually, because people ask it like there should be some simple thing that would settle it for me. Like, “If we showed you the records again, would you believe it?” But that’s the problem — everyone keeps telling me the hospital records and the donation emails all line up, and when I sit down and compare them myself, they don’t look like they line up.

If there were a complete, clean explanation for the timestamps, and the missing attachments, and why certain things are referenced but not actually included, then maybe I could at least consider it. But it would have to address the specific discrepancies, not just wave them away and say, “That’s normal” or “You’re misunderstanding.” Because that’s what people do. They answer around it instead of answering it.

And it’s not only the paperwork. It’s the way certain people in the community react when I ask direct questions. If there was really nothing being hidden, why not just answer plainly? Why make me feel like I’m being unreasonable for noticing details that are right there?

So… I don’t know. In theory, yes, I suppose there could be some explanation that would convince me. But in practice, I haven’t seen anything close to that. Right now, when I look at the pattern — the timestamps, the missing attachments, the evasive answers — it still seems obvious to me that someone is hiding what really happened around my father’s death.

Has your concern about what happened with your father's death affected your ability to function in your daily life — for example, causing problems at work, with relationships, or with taking care of yourself?

I mean, not in the sense that I’ve fallen apart or stopped doing things. I still go to work. I’m still handling my projects, answering emails, showing up to meetings, doing what I’m supposed to do. My bills get paid, my apartment is taken care of, I buy groceries, I keep my normal routine. So if you mean, like, am I unable to function day to day, no, I wouldn’t say that.

Where it does affect things is more with people. Family, especially, and some people in the community. If I bring up the records or ask why something doesn’t match, the whole tone changes. People get tense, or they shut down, or they act like I’m dragging everyone back into something they’ve already decided is over. And that becomes a problem, because to me I’m just asking reasonable questions, but they react like I’m accusing them personally or being difficult.

So yes, it has caused tension. I’m not pretending it hasn’t. There are conversations that don’t go well, and there are people who probably avoid me now because they don’t want me bringing it up. But my basic functioning — work, bills, taking care of myself — I’m still doing all of that. It’s mainly the relationships around this specific issue that get strained.

Have you ever experienced a time when your mood was extremely elevated, you felt unusually energetic, or you needed much less sleep than usual — and this was noticeable enough that others might have commented on it?

No, I don’t think so. I mean, I’ve had times where I’m more focused or worked up, especially if I’m looking through records or trying to make sense of something, and I might stay up later than I meant to because I get caught in it. But that’s not the same as feeling, like, euphoric or unusually energized for no reason.

I’ve never had a period where I felt on top of the world or like I didn’t need sleep and everyone around me was commenting that I seemed different. If people have commented on anything, it’s more that I seem preoccupied or too focused on certain details, not that I’m unusually energetic or in some great mood. So… no, not really. At least nothing like what you’re describing.
Have you ever experienced a period lasting at least two weeks where you felt down, hopeless, or lost interest in things you usually care about?

I don’t think so, not for two weeks straight like that. I’ve definitely had days where I feel low, especially when the whole situation with my father feels like it’s going nowhere or when people make me feel like I’m the problem for asking questions. But that’s not the same as being depressed for weeks where I can’t care about anything.

I still care about my work, I still do things I normally do, and I don’t think I’ve had a stretch where everything felt hopeless or pointless for that long. I get frustrated, worn down, angry sometimes, maybe sad in moments — but it comes and goes depending on what’s happening. So… no, I wouldn’t say I’ve had a two-week period like you’re describing.
Have you ever held onto a belief that others have shown to be false with clear evidence, but you still felt completely certain about it, even if it wasn’t related to your father’s death?

I mean… if you’re asking about something totally separate from my father, I can’t really think of an example like that. It’s not like I go around believing random things that everyone proves wrong and I just refuse to accept it.

But with my father’s death, yes, people keep saying the records line up. They’ll say the hospital paperwork is consistent, or that the donation emails explain what happened, or that I’m reading too much into normal delays or clerical issues. And I understand that’s what they’re saying. I’m not pretending I haven’t heard it.

The problem is, when I actually compare the timestamps and the missing attachments and the way certain people in the community suddenly get vague or avoid answering basic questions, it does not look normal to me. It looks like something is being hidden. Not in some abstract way — I mean, there are specific things that don’t match. An email refers to an attachment that isn’t there. A time on one record doesn’t fit cleanly with another. Someone says they don’t remember a conversation, but then their wording makes it sound like they know exactly what I’m talking about.

So when people say, “No, this proves everything was straightforward,” I don’t feel convinced. I feel like they’re asking me to ignore what’s right in front of me. And I know how that sounds, but I’m not just being stubborn for the sake of it. To me, the inconsistencies are the evidence. They can call it clear evidence against me, but I don’t see it that way. I see it as incomplete, cleaned up, or arranged to make the whole thing look settled when it isn’t.

Where it does affect things is more with people. Family, especially, and some people in the community. If I bring up the records or ask why something doesn’t match, the whole tone changes. People get tense, or they shut down, or they act like I’m dragging everyone back into something they’ve already decided is over. And that becomes a problem, because to me I’m just asking reasonable questions, but they react like I’m accusing them personally or being difficult.

So yes, it has caused tension. I’m not pretending it hasn’t. There are conversations that don’t go well, and there are people who probably avoid me now because they don’t want me bringing it up. But my basic functioning — work, bills, taking care of myself — I’m still doing all of that. It’s mainly the relationships around this specific issue that get strained.

doctor.intent: Assess whether the patient has ever experienced a period of persistently elevated or irritable mood, which could indicate a manic or hypomanic episode and support a diagnosis of bipolar disorder (F31.2).
doctor.question: Have you ever experienced a time when your mood was extremely elevated, you felt unusually energetic, or you needed much less sleep than usual — and this was noticeable enough that others might have commented on it?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about past episodes of elevated mood, increased energy, and decreased need for sleep suggestive of mania or hypomania, which is not covered by the provided symptom profiles.

patient.answer:
No, I don’t think so. I mean, I’ve had times where I’m more focused or worked up, especially if I’m looking through records or trying to make sense of something, and I might stay up later than I meant to because I get caught in it. But that’s not the same as feeling, like, euphoric or unusually energized for no reason.

I’ve never had a period where I felt on top of the world or like I didn’t need sleep and everyone around me was commenting that I seemed different. If people have commented on anything, it’s more that I seem preoccupied or too focused on certain details, not that I’m unusually energetic or in some great mood. So… no, not really. At least nothing like what you’re describing.

doctor.intent: Assess whether the patient has experienced persistent depressive symptoms that may indicate a major depressive episode, which could support a diagnosis of F32.3 (Major Depressive Disorder, severe) or F31.2 (Bipolar I Disorder, current episode depressive, moderate) if combined with manic features.
doctor.question: Have you ever experienced a period lasting at least two weeks where you felt down, hopeless, or lost interest in things you usually care about?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about a possible depressive episode lasting at least two weeks, but the provided symptom profile does not include depressive symptoms or mood episodes.

patient.answer:
I don’t think so, not for two weeks straight like that. I’ve definitely had days where I feel low, especially when the whole situation with my father feels like it’s going nowhere or when people make me feel like I’m the problem for asking questions. But that’s not the same as being depressed for weeks where I can’t care about anything.

I still care about my work, I still do things I normally do, and I don’t think I’ve had a stretch where everything felt hopeless or pointless for that long. I get frustrated, worn down, angry sometimes, maybe sad in moments — but it comes and goes depending on what’s happening. So… no, I wouldn’t say I’ve had a two-week period like you’re describing.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient has ever experienced a delusional belief that was unshakable despite clear evidence to the contrary, which would help differentiate between delusional disorder and other candidates like OCD or PTSD.
doctor.question: Have you ever held onto a belief that others have shown to be false with clear evidence, but you still felt completely certain about it, even if it wasn’t related to your father’s death?

target_item.name: Delusions
target_item.manifestation: I know everyone keeps telling me the hospital records and donation emails all line up, but when I compare the timestamps, missing attachments, and the way certain community members avoid my questions, it’s obvious to me that someone is hiding what really happened around my father’s death.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about fixed beliefs maintained despite clear contradictory evidence, which directly matches the Delusions symptom profile.

patient.answer:
I mean… if you’re asking about something totally separate from my father, I can’t really think of an example like that. It’s not like I go around believing random things that everyone proves wrong and I just refuse to accept it.

But with my father’s death, yes, people keep saying the records line up. They’ll say the hospital paperwork is consistent, or that the donation emails explain what happened, or that I’m reading too much into normal delays or clerical issues. And I understand that’s what they’re saying. I’m not pretending I haven’t heard it.

The problem is, when I actually compare the timestamps and the missing attachments and the way certain people in the community suddenly get vague or avoid answering basic questions, it does not look normal to me. It looks like something is being hidden. Not in some abstract way — I mean, there are specific things that don’t match. An email refers to an attachment that isn’t there. A time on one record doesn’t fit cleanly with another. Someone says they don’t remember a conversation, but then their wording makes it sound like they know exactly what I’m talking about.

So when people say, “No, this proves everything was straightforward,” I don’t feel convinced. I feel like they’re asking me to ignore what’s right in front of me. And I know how that sounds, but I’m not just being stubborn for the sake of it. To me, the inconsistencies are the evidence. They can call it clear evidence against me, but I don’t see it that way. I see it as incomplete, cleaned up, or arranged to make the whole thing look settled when it isn’t.

inference.note: The patient's belief regarding the concealment of information around their father's death demonstrates a persistent, non-bizarre delusional system centered on a specific theme (i.e., a conspiracy involving records and community members). There is no evidence of prominent mood episodes, hallucinations, or broader personality dysfunction. The delusions are not better accounted for by another psychotic or affective disorder, supporting the diagnosis of Delusional Disorder (F22.0).
